note: The Board maps what is in dispute onto what is in the record. FACT nodes are events in the court record (that testimony occurred is a fact, whether it is TRUE is for the jury). QUESTION nodes are what the jury must decide. COMMUNITY nodes are user-submitted and appear only after review. An edge says how one node bears on another, and who advances that argument.

nodes.title: THE question: Was Clancy criminally responsible on Jan 24, 2023?
nodes.body: Under Commonwealth v. McHoul, she is not responsible if mental disease or defect left her without substantial capacity either to appreciate wrongfulness OR to conform her conduct to law. The Commonwealth must prove responsibility beyond a reasonable doubt.

nodes.title: Will involuntary manslaughter be on the verdict slip?
nodes.body: Defense wants it as a lesser option; prosecution says specific intent to kill forecloses it. Ruling pending as jury instructions are finalized.

nodes.title: Uncontested: Clancy caused the deaths
nodes.body: Defense counsel in openings: she 'is aware that she killed her children and is not trying to deny that.' The trial is about criminal responsibility, not identity.

nodes.title: Resnick (defense): postpartum psychosis, command hallucinations
nodes.body: 'Altruistic filicide — a murder committed out of love, rather than hostility.' 'Psychosis can indeed wax and wane.' Evaluated her four months after the deaths.

nodes.title: Zeizel (defense): could not tell right from wrong
nodes.body: Saw Clancy ~60 times over three years. 'Intrusive thoughts are unrelenting.' Concluded she 'was unable to conform her behavior to the rule of law' on Jan 24.

nodes.title: The reported voice
nodes.body: Zeizel: she reported 'a male voice ordering her' that she 'had no choice but to kill her children. And kill herself.' Chaplain Cavanaugh: a 'persistent' male voice threatening her and the children's safety.

nodes.title: Mack (rebuttal): depression, not psychosis
nodes.body: Interviewed Clancy twice in April 2026. Major depressive disorder; she 'methodically killed her children one by one' while knowing it was wrong and could have stopped. 'I don't know that that feeling or that belief is necessarily psychotic.'

nodes.title: Tufts: 'no signs of psychosis' the day before
nodes.body: Her treating psychiatrist saw no psychosis or mania at the Jan 23 telehealth visit; Clancy denied suicidal or homicidal ideation. Cross: 14 visits all telehealth, limited postpartum experience, never got other providers' records.

nodes.title: The digital record
nodes.body: Phone/laptop forensics: 'ketamine for suicide ideation' (Jan 18), 'symptoms of postpartum psychosis' (Jan 19), 'Can you treat a sociopath' (Jan 20), a suicide-methods page visit (Aug 2022), and an Oct 25, 2022 note: 'I'm sad and depressed. I can't parent my 3rd child like my first.'

nodes.title: Prosecution's planning theory
nodes.body: Openings: she searched routes and takeout, took the children to the basement, strangled them with exercise bands. Whiffin's Apple Health data: stair climbs 5:33/5:38 p.m. Theory: she wanted to 'take them with her.'

nodes.title: The clinicians who saw no danger to the children
nodes.body: Jollotta: suicidal ideation documented, but 'never had thoughts on harming her children.' Paul: intake denied ideation; sleep was the concern. Dukes: 'frequent suicide ideation' Dec 2, improved by Dec 9. The pediatrician saw Cora that morning — routine.

nodes.title: The medication thread
nodes.body: Defense: '13 different psychiatric medications' prescribed; involuntary intoxication through over-prescription. Toxicology: 4–5 benzodiazepines in her system, mostly therapeutic levels; one 'a little elevated.' Her mother: 'The medication was pretty much just destroying her mind.'

nodes.title: RESOLVED: the McLean TikTok dispute
nodes.body: A former McLean social worker posted a TikTok disputing the prosecution's 'premier medical institution' framing and was proposed as a defense witness. Judge Sullivan found her credible but excluded the testimony for 'limited materiality.' How a viral claim met the record: it got a hearing, and a ruling.
